Presentation by MRS JOSHI
WITNESS:  So just to reiterate, my name is Cathy Joshi,
I'm one of the technical experts.  I've been looking at
the structural and architectural matters on this
dispute.
Next slide, please.
Next slide, please.
In my presentation today, I'm going to focus on the
following key issues: the leakages through the expansion
joints; the traffic coating; the Laminam cladding; and
then three other issues: plaza finishes, steelwork and
glass doors.
Next slide, please.  Above, please.  Thank you.
Just I wanted to clarify one of the matters that
there appears to have been some confusion on with regard
to the defects.  In the joint statement, Dr Brade and
I agreed there are four possible routes of water into
the basement.  And I'd just like you to think of the
basement as a big concrete box that is waterproofed all
the way round it.
One of the defects I'll be discussing is the water
leakages through the expansion joints, which come
through the top, and that's landscaping and plaza paving
level.  So that's the downward arrows on this diagram.
On the left, the water leakage laterally through
the retaining walls: that's covered in my reports and
the joint statement.  The water leakage upwards through
the basement floor slab: I'm going to discuss that in
relation to the impact on the traffic coating
installation.  And then on the right-hand side, the
water entering from the ramps.  This is not a defect in
the counterclaim and I won't be discussing this in
my presentation.
Next slide, please.
So first of all, I'll be looking at the leakages
through the expansion joints.
Next slide, please.
So just to clarify, and apologies if you do
understand this, but I thought it would be useful just
to explain what the expansion joint area is.
So the blue lines in the top sketch indicate the
approximate locations of the expansion joints in the
podium slab.  So there are multiple expansion joints
running all across the slab.
In the bottom image, it's a photograph of the site.
I've coloured the buildings in yellow and the podium
area in blue, because the podium area is where the
rainfall occurs, and the expansion joint leakages have
occurred underneath those areas where there's rainfall.
So if you superimposed these two diagrams, you would
get the expansion joints through the podium areas, and
that's where these defects have occurred.
Next slide, please.
So expansion joints are basically gaps in the
concrete slab which allow movement of the slabs due to
temperature changes, moisture changes and load
variations.  The expansion joints are waterproofed to
stop water coming through them, and there has been
a number of details included during this project.  This
is one of the details from the approved waterproofing
shop drawings, which shows one of the expansion joint
details.  There's quite a few varieties of these, but
this is one of the more typical ones.
You'll see in the bottom left enlarged diagram
the expansion joint is 15mm.  It's typically filled by
a filler board.  The filler board does no more than just
fill the gap.  And then there's details of how the
expansion joint is protected by waterproofing protection
board and other build-ups around it.
So I'm going to -- if we go to the next slide,
please -- look at detail B, which is at the top of that.
What you can see -- and I've enlarged the labels in
the diagram on the right-hand side -- is that there is
a layer of 5mm bituminous membrane.  Above that
membrane, there's an additional two layers of Torchseal
black membrane.  So there's three layers of
waterproofing that run along the top of the expansion
joints.  There's a small circle, which is the turbo
sealant, and that just basically acts as a bead to lay
the waterproofing across.
You'll see that the waterproofing has a slight lap
above that round sealant circle, and that's because the
waterproofing has to have some give in it, so that if
the slabs move away from each other, the waterproofing
is not put under any force; it has the ability to move
in and out quite freely.
Above the waterproofing layers, there's a protection
screed and there's also a protection board.
So this is basically how the expansion joint detail
was put in the drawings and in the method statement.  If
the expansion joint waterproofing had been installed in
accordance with this approved detail, it would be
watertight and there would be no water leakage through
into the basement.
So it's agreed, common ground, that the
specification section 07100 for waterproofing requires
an extended warranty of 10 years for waterproofing, and
this warranty was provided by the waterproofing
specialist, Al Shirawi.
If installed correctly, it's difficult to damage
that build-up above the membrane and the membrane
itself.  Any damage that did occur is unlikely to
penetrate through all the layers of build-up, so three
layers of waterproofing membrane, the protection screed,
the protection board, and then whatever backfill and
finishes you have on top.
So the membrane is protected by these boards and
layers of finishes.  So if there is any damage to the
waterproofing, it's likely to have occurred at the time
of installation, when CSCEC was still responsible for
the site.
And just so you're aware that the build-up between
the waterproofing and the top of the finishes varies
between 30cm and probably about 1m across the site,
depending on what the levels are above.  But at all
locations you have the protection screed, the protection
board, three layers of waterproofing and then
the finishes and backfill on top.
Next slide, please.
So it was the responsibility of the contractor to
provide an integrated site-wide waterproofing system,
and part of that involved water testing of the
waterproofing.  But not all the expansion joints were
subject to water integrity testing; instead, testing was
just carried out at a few locations randomly selected by
the engineer.
So I've shown two examples of the testing.
Basically, a bund is put around the area of an expansion
joint and water is placed within the bund, and it's left
to see if there's any leakage.
So there were -- I think it was either five or
seven; apologies, I don't recall the exact number.  But
there were very few areas of the expansion joint tested.
And if you recall the diagram I showed you of the whole
site and number of expansion joints, I haven't seen any
evidence that the full expansion joints were tested at
the time of installation.
Next slide, please.
So just going back, I've taken the detail and just
added some colour, just to clarify what happens to
the expansion joint above the waterproofing layer.
So on the left, the concrete is coloured in blue;
the filler board and the expansion joint in yellow; and
you'll see the small green circle, which is the backer
rod, which basically is just there to support
the waterproofing.  The red layer across the top of that
is the waterproofing layer, the three layers of
waterproofing across the expansion joints.
On the right is an enlargement of the top of that
detail.  So from the waterproofing layer upwards to the
top of the finishes, the expansion joint carries on up
to the top, which allows movement to carry on all the
way up to the surface.  But that top, between the
waterproofing layer and the top of the podium finishes,
is some form of compressible sealant or compressible
material.  It's not a waterproofing layer; it's just
something to fill the gap that's compressible, to take
the finish all the way up to the surface.
Next slide, please.
So I'm going to talk about the impact of ponding
above the expansion joints.
If you look at the diagram again on the right -- and
apologies for the repetition, but it's very important to
understand where the waterproofing membrane sits in
the detail on the expansion joint.  The red line in the
diagram on the right shows where the waterproofing
membrane is, and again we've got the lap to allow some
movement and we have the three layers of waterproofing
membrane.  So this is from the method statement.  So
the barrier between the water at the podium level and
the expansion joint gap is at that red line, so it's
below the backfill and the finishes of the podium.
So ponding on the plaza has no impact on the leaking
through the expansion joints, because the design intent
is for the water barrier to be at that level of the
membrane.  The plaza finishes themselves have not been
designed to be a water barrier.  So water ingress cannot
be contributing to ponding in the plaza above the
basement; it will only have an impact if there's
a defect in that waterproofing which allows water to
pass through it.
If the waterproofing was installed as per the
approved method statement and drawings, there would be
no penetration or holes in the waterproofing and the
water would simply not pass through to the expansion
joints.  So leakages into the basement through the
expansion joints only happen where there are defects in
the waterproofing system.
If the expansion joints were constructed to comply
with the approved details, extreme weather events would
not cause water leakages into the basement through the
expansion joints, any more than light rainfall would.
Three layers of waterproofing membrane is a very robust
waterproofing system and would not allow water to
penetrate.
The increased rainfall would not impact the ability
of the project to withstand water ingress.  So going
back to the concrete box, that's waterproofed around.
Extreme rainfall would not impact -- if the
waterproofing was correctly installed, would not impact
the ability of the project to withstand water ingress
from the top, above the podium finishes.  There might be
more water accumulating on the plaza paving and that
might take longer to drain away, but it should not
penetrate through to the expansion joints.
Next slide, please.
So the first record of leakages through the
expansion joints was in the Young report, which was
issued in March 2020, which includes details of leakages
from expansion joints after rain in November and
December 2019.  So it records that these leakages were
first noted.
But also it records, in the second paragraph on that
page, that it was "hard to give [an] exact reason for
the leakages" because all the expansion joints and the
leak points were "covered with ... paving, landscaping
and other finishing material".  So once the protection
board, the protection screed, the backfill and the
finishes are in place, there's no way to see that
waterproofing.
Young Engineering said, based on their experience:
"... there are high[] chances of damage[] [to]
the existing water proofing system over [the] expansion
joint[s]."
Next slide, please.
So leakages were noted in the TOC documents of
July 2020, when they recorded that there was leakage
through the expansion joints at upper ground slab,
resulting in water ponding at a few locations.  And
again, in the DLC of December 2021, there was the record
that there was water leakage from some of the expansion
joints.
Next slide, please.
Bureau Veritas issued a report: it was revised in
September 2020, March 2021, and the final version issued
in January 2022.  This report included photographic
records of leakages from the expansion joints in many
locations.  And I've included some examples where you
can see water dropping from the expansion joints and
the water in the car park which has fallen from
the expansion joints.
Next slide, please.
There's also a number of records of ongoing
leakages, which I've included some photographic examples
of it.  So March 2022 records "Water leak issues ...
[in] many locations"; and then records of February 2022
and November 2023, leaks from expansion joints are also
photographed and recorded.
Next slide, please.
In February and March 2024, there was another report
issued which had photographic evidence of leaks from
expansion joints.
Next slide, please.
I visited the site in January 2025 and April 2025.
It was a dry period in Dubai, but I could see on the
columns there was yellow staining, which indicated that
water had come through from the expansion joints.  The
reason that the leakage is sometimes shown, I think,
yellow on the columns is because the filler board
I showed on the diagrams earlier quite often has bitumen
in it, and that will wash through and cause yellow
staining.  But that's the only reason for the yellow
staining.
I also visited the site on 14 December 2025.  There
had been a light rainfall the day before, and I was able
to observe probably about 10 to 12 locations -- I've
included some examples in this presentation, in my
report -- but there was water leakages from
the expansion joints visible in the car park.
Next slide, please.
Then a report from DIEZA on 18 and 19 December.
Unfortunately I wasn't able to get to site on that day,
but they recorded leakages in more than 100 locations,
and that's almost all of the columns in the basement,
after the rainfall.
Next slide, please.
So the metal trays.  If you look on the right-hand
side, I've included a photograph with a small blue arrow
just showing what the metal trays are.  The contractor
installed the metal trays below the expansion joints to
collect any residue or water percolating through the
expansion joints.  And they basically go from column to
column and they are small trays -- the middle photograph
at the bottom is a cross-section of one of them -- fixed
to the underside of the concrete, and they are basically
collecting the water.
So these trays were installed before March 2020,
because they're mentioned in the Young report of that
date as already being in place.  They weren't part of
the original design or contract documentation.
If the expansion joint waterproofing had been
installed and protected in accordance with the approved
details, these metal trays would not be necessary.  They
only became necessary because there were leaks from
the expansion joints.  They were not approved by the
engineer, and to my knowledge, they have not been
approved by the engineer at all.
And they were considered just a temporary solution
to the leakages from the expansion joints.  There are
some minutes of meetings from March 2020 when they are
spoken about as a temporary solution while a permanent
solution to the leakage is sorted out.
Next slide, please.
So based on the evidence I've seen, no excavations
have been carried out to identify the root cause of the
defects.  The only way the root cause of this defect can
be established is by excavating the finishes and the
backfill above the expansion joints, removing the
protection screed, removing the protection board and
exposing the waterproofing layers.  There is no other
way to identify the root cause.
The water trays do not resolve the ongoing leakages
at the column junctions, as demonstrated by the area of
the leakages adjacent to the columns after the rainfall
in December 2025.  The water trays which were envisaged
as a temporary solution are still there, but they just
can't cope with the amount of water ingress after
rainfall.
To resolve the water leakage issue, remedial works
are required for the expansion joints, for the
waterproofing of expansion joints, not for the joints in
the plaza paving.
Based on my experience of similar expansion joint
defects on other projects and the evidence of extensive
leakages during the rainfall of 18 to 19 December 2025,
it is my recommendation that rectification to all
expansion joints be carried out to prevent further
damage to the project from water ingress.
So each of the water trays runs between two columns,
and in the reports from DIEZA of December 2025
it appears that there was water at almost every column,
which would indicate that there's probably expansion
joint defects between every column as well.
The metal trays obscure the expansion joints, so
the exact location of the defects cannot be seen from
the underside of the slab.  The only way to identify the
defects, as I said previously, is to excavate down from
the plaza level and investigate at all locations.  And
the rectification works would require repair of the
expansion joints and the waterproofing detail to comply
with the contract requirements and approved submittals.
Next slide, please.
So that was the leakage through the expansion
joints.  I'll now move on to the traffic coating.
Next slide, please.
The traffic coating is specified under
specification 07180, which describes it as
a "polyurethane waterproofing and protective traffic
deck coating".  The specification doesn't say gloss
finish or what the finish should be.
The approved product required by the specification
is Masterseal Traffic 1332, although a finish from
National Paints was used.
And the specification is part of the moisture and
thermal protection division 7.  It's not part of
division 9 finishes, which would indicate that it's
decorative only.
So the coating should form an impermeable barrier to
water infiltration.  And this is quite typical for
traffic coating because it safeguards traffic's concrete
substrates from deterioration caused by moisture and
chemicals.
Part 3 of the specification section 07180 describes
the execution of the traffic coating, starting with the
inspection and preparation of the surface.  The surfaces
were to be free of debris and dirt, and the substrates
were to be powerfloated to remove all contaminants and
impurities detrimental to the bonding of the traffic
coating system.
The specification includes a requirement for
a 10-year warranty, and this 10-year warranty requires
the repair and replacement of:
"... traffic coating which has blistered,
delaminated, separated from [the] substrate materials,
deteriorated, split due to development of cracks wider
than 1.6 mm in [the] substrate, [or] lost aggregate
sufficient to expose the waterproofing membrane
component ..."
So it's quite wide-ranging, the warranty
requirements.
Next slide, please.
So as I said, National Paints provided the material,
and the method statement submitted by National Paints
also had a requirement for surface preparation, which
reflected the requirement in the specification itself.
The method statement included a requirement for
the new concrete floors to have a moisture content not
exceeding 5%.  I haven't seen any records to show
whether the moisture content was tested.  It would have
to have been tested at that time, before the traffic
coating was installed.
I have seen records to show that the traffic coating
was generally inspected and approved at the time of
installation.  Based on the inspection requests I've
seen, these inspections were carried out between January
and December 2019, with some later inspections in
February and June 2020.
Next slide, please.
So in my reports I conclude that dampness is
a probable cause of the defects.  My opinion is that to
the extent I am able, based on evidence I've seen,
I agree with the conclusions in the Bureau Veritas
report that the peeling of the traffic coating was and
is due to the dampness of the substrate; the peeling-off
of paint was and is due to poor workmanship of concrete
repair of the substrate; there's evidence of poor
workmanship for the substrate surface preparation; and
there was a general failure of the waterproofing system.
And I concluded that I was of the opinion -- am of
the opinion -- that all areas of the traffic coating
were potentially exposed to moisture/water coming up
from the concrete substrate -- so that's the concrete
box, the moisture coming up -- and also coming down
from the water ingress through the expansion joints.
So I'm now going to explain why the dampness and
the surface preparation are the probable causes of
the peeling-off of the paint.
Next slide, please.
So what happens when the dewatering is switched off?
It's common ground that the dewatering was switched off
during February or March 2019.  So as I've just said,
the inspection requests I've seen for the traffic
coating were between January and December 2019, so
across the period when the dewatering was switched off.
The groundwater level is above the level of the
basement slab.  So when the dewatering is switched off,
there's a hydrostatic head of water which tries to force
its way into the basement.
The dewatering system uses a series of pits and
holes, and after it's switched off, these holes and pits
need to be sealed and waterproofed.
So the Young Engineering report of March 2020
describes these waterproofing details.  Again, there's
a diagram on the right-hand side taken from that report.
There's two layers of modified membrane and then there's
another layer of -- sorry, three overlapped layers of
Proofex membrane and protection board.
This is just one example of the detail.  These
requirements are also in the specification section 07110
and in the shop drawings.  But basically, there's
a process to happen after the dewaterings are switched
off, which will take some time, to make sure that all
the pits and holes used for the dewatering are sealed
and waterproofed.
Next slide, please.
So any water seepage present during or prior to
application of the epoxy could indicate the slab was not
adequately dry or watertight.  So the Bureau Veritas
reports included photographs of water seepage from below
the traffic coating and of areas where water seepage was
being treated using injections.  I've included some
examples here where you can see water seepage below
the traffic coating and where you can see they --
the yellow is where they are repairing the water seepage
using injections.
Next slide, please.
Leakages were noted in both the TOC of July 2020 and
the DLC, and the Young report of March 2020 also
included photos of water seepage and injection work in
progress.
In April 2021, it was recorded there were still
dewatering issues at the lower ground level, some water
still coming in at some locations.  And the epoxy was
recorded as one of the defects in the DLC.
Next slide, please.
So looking now at what evidence we have of
the traffic coating defects, the Bureau Veritas report
includes photos of areas where the traffic coating was
peeling off surfaces and cracks in the epoxy floor
paints.  Now, just going back to the specification, this
is a waterproofing polyurethane system which should be
continuous, and should not be flaking or cracking like
this.
Next slide, please.
On the left-hand side, we've got examples from
the Bureau Veritas report, which includes examples of
concrete repair.  So where there were cracks in the
concrete or water ingress, they repaired the concrete
using injection and other methods, and these repairs
were carried on in areas which already had traffic
coating in place.
On the right-hand side, the Young report includes
similar examples of repairs ongoing, some of which are
quite major repairs, and they're ongoing in areas where
the traffic coating had already been applied.
Next slide, please.
I visited the site on 13 January 2025 and I noticed
many areas of traffic coating with paint flaking off,
significantly larger than dinner plates, some quite
large areas where the epoxy had just flaked away.  If
you look at the top-right image, you'll see that the
edges have actually lifted, and it looks like that
traffic coating has not bonded to the surface below
at all.
Next slide, please.
DIEZA FM did a report in December 2025, and these
are examples of some of the photographs again showing
quite large areas of epoxy flaking off and missing.
Next slide, please.
During my visit of 14 December 2025, I observed
the left-hand image, which shows an area of epoxy
missing but also shows multiple cracks in the area.  So
not only is that piece of epoxy missing, but it looks
like the surrounding areas have failed as well and
the epoxy would be flaking off in the future.
Similarly, the images on the right show cracking
around missing epoxy -- particularly the image on the
right-hand side, you can see a large crack running
down -- which indicates it's not only the area where the
epoxy is missing but there are other defects that are
underneath the epoxy, and it's not bonded to this slab.
Next slide, please.
I just want to make the point that there have been
ongoing repairs to the epoxy by DIEZA FM over the period
since I've been involved and before, and therefore any
visit to the site, the expert will only have observed
the defects visible on the day of the inspections.
There were different defects on the days between my
inspections: that's because the FM is doing ongoing
repairs to try and keep up with the epoxy defects.
In my experience, traffic coating does not debond
and peel off in the manner that I've observed on the
site and in the photographic evidence.  The failures
I've seen indicate there are application or material
defects in the epoxy coating and it's not just normal
wear and tear.
My opinion is that the failure of the traffic
coating is due to lack of bonding with the substrate due
to poor workmanship and moisture content, and
the traffic coating should be fully replaced.
A 10-year warranty was issued by CSCEC, not by
National Paints.  I'm not sure they have -- there's some
evidence as to why that happened, but I'm not clear the
reason for that.  But that's not within my remit anyway.
Patch repairs that have been ongoing have caused
a patchwork effect -- you can see an example on the
photograph on the right -- which is not aesthetically
acceptable for a recently completed project.  It's very
difficult to match patches of epoxy coating like this to
other areas that have been in place for a while.
Prior to the re-application of the traffic coating,
the leaks from the expansion joints and the excess
moisture content of the slab are to be resolved and
the substrate should be properly prepared.
Next slide, please.
I'll now move on to the Laminam.
Next slide, please.
So the original specification for the cladding
system was for stone cladding with mechanical fixings.
The specification following value-engineering was wall
cladding with "Dry or Wet Fixing".  The cladding that is
